title: Statistics Grade 6: Mean, Median, Mode, Range and Graphs + Free Quiz
meta_title: Statistics Grade 6: Mean, Median, Mode + Quiz
meta_desc: Master statistics grade 6: find mean, median, mode and range, and read bar graphs, dot plots and frequency tables. Free 8-question quiz inside.
excerpt: Grade 6 statistics is really two skills wearing one name: summarising a data set with mean, median, mode and range, and pulling answers out of a bar graph or dot plot. Here is how to practise both, plus a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Here is a data set a Grade 6 student can actually picture: the runs a cricketer scored in five matches — 20, 35, 35, 10 and 50. Ask for the ‘average’ and most children add and divide fine. Ask which score was typical, or which came up most often, or how spread out the scores were, and the room goes quiet. That gap is exactly what statistics grade 6 is about. It is really two skills sharing one chapter name: summarising a data set with mean, median, mode and range, and then reading answers straight off a bar graph, dot plot or frequency table.

I have taught this to a lot of eleven-year-olds, and the mistake is almost never the arithmetic. It is not knowing which number the question is asking for. So let us pin down each one with the same small data set, then practise reading it off a picture.

The four numbers that describe a data set

Take those five cricket scores again: 20, 35, 35, 10, 50. Four different questions, four different answers.

  • Mean — add every value and divide by how many there are. (20 + 35 + 35 + 10 + 50) = 150, and 150 ÷ 5 = 30. The mean is 30.
  • Median — the middle value once the data is sorted. Sorted: 10, 20, 35, 35, 50. The middle one is 35.
  • Mode — the value that appears most often. 35 shows up twice, everything else once, so the mode is 35.
  • Range — the gap between the biggest and smallest. 50 − 10 = 40.

Notice the mean (30) and the median (35) are different here, and that is the whole point — they are answering different questions.

The step everyone forgets: sort first

You cannot find the median of an unsorted list. The single most common slip I see is a child grabbing the middle number of the data as written instead of after sorting. Always line the numbers up smallest to largest first. If there is an even count — say six values — the median is the mean of the two middle ones. That is the one wrinkle Grade 6 adds beyond the basic idea.

Why statistics grade 6 uses more than the mean

The mean is famous, but it can lie. Imagine five friends have pocket money of ₹10, ₹10, ₹10, ₹10 and ₹460. The mean is ₹100 — a number nobody actually has. The median (₹10) describes the group far better because one huge value has dragged the mean upward. Teaching a child to notice when an outlier is fooling the mean is a genuine Grade 6 win, and it is the sort of reasoning question that shows up in good worksheets.

Reading data from graphs and tables

The second half of the chapter is picture work. Grade 6 focuses on three displays, and each answers questions slightly differently.

DisplayBest forHow to read it
Frequency tableCounting how often each value occursThe tally or number column gives the frequency of each category
Bar graphComparing categories at a glanceRead the height of each bar against the scale on the axis
Dot plotSeeing the shape and mode of a small data setCount the dots stacked above each value; the tallest stack is the mode

Watch the scale

On a bar graph the axis might climb in 2s, 5s or 10s, not 1s. A bar sitting halfway between the 20 and 30 gridlines is 25, not 21. Before answering anything, I make students say out loud what one gridline is worth. It sounds trivial; it fixes about half of all graph mistakes.

Dot plots quietly hand you the mode

A dot plot is my favourite bridge between the two halves of this chapter. Each dot is one data point, stacked above its value. The tallest column is instantly the mode, the leftmost and rightmost dots give you the range, and you can even total the dots to work back to a mean. One picture, and suddenly all four summary numbers are within reach.

A practice routine that actually builds the skill

Skill practice beats re-reading definitions. What works for the parents I know is short and mixed:

  • Give a set of 5 to 7 numbers and ask for all four measures — mean, median, mode, range — in one go, so the child has to choose the right method each time.
  • Then flip it: show a small bar graph or dot plot and ask the same four questions from the picture.
  • Once a week, throw in one outlier question — ‘which measure describes this group best, and why?’ — to build the judgement, not just the calculation.

One honest caveat: do not drill mean, median and mode as three unrelated recipes. A child who can compute all three but cannot say which one answers ‘what is typical here?’ has memorised, not understood. The choosing is the skill.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

The free eight-question quiz below mixes both halves of the chapter — some pure calculation of mean, median, mode and range, and some reading straight off a table or dot plot. Let your child try it, then read the explanations together for anything missed. When they are ready for longer graded practice, the printable worksheet at the end gives plenty of data sets and graph questions, each with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 6 Statistics Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on mean, median, mode, range and reading graphs and tables. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 6 mean, median, mode, range and data graphs

questions.explanation: Add them: 4 + 8 + 6 + 2 = 20. There are 4 values, so 20 ÷ 4 = 5.
Sort first: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. The middle value is 5.
The value 5 appears three times, more than any other, so the mode is 5.

questions.q: A dot plot shows 3 dots above 6, 1 above 7 and 2 above 8. What is the mode?
questions.explanation: The tallest stack of dots is above 6 (three dots), so 6 occurs most often and is the mode.

questions.q: On a bar graph the scale rises in 5s. A bar reaches halfway between 15 and 20. What value is it?
questions.explanation: Halfway between 15 and 20 is 17.5. Always check what one gridline is worth before reading a bar.

questions.q: Which measure is the middle value of a sorted data set?
questions.explanation: The median is the middle value once the data is arranged from smallest to largest.

questions.q: A frequency table shows Red 4, Blue 6, Green 6, Yellow 2. What is the mode colour?
questions.explanation: Both Blue and Green have the highest frequency (6 each), so the data has two modes: Blue and Green.

faq.q: What topics are in Grade 6 statistics?
faq.a: Grade 6 covers summarising a data set with mean, median, mode and range, plus organising and reading data from frequency tables, bar graphs and dot plots. The skill is choosing the right measure and reading a scale correctly.

faq.q: What is the difference between mean, median and mode?
faq.a: The mean is the total divided by how many values there are, the median is the middle value after sorting, and the mode is the value that appears most often. They answer different questions, so a data set can have three different ‘averages’.

faq.q: How do you find the median of an even number of values?
faq.a: Sort the numbers, then take the two in the middle and find their mean. For 4, 6, 9, 11 the two middle values are 6 and 9, so the median is (6 + 9) ÷ 2 = 7.5.

faq.q: Why does an outlier matter in statistics?
faq.a: A single very large or very small value can pull the mean far away from what is typical, while the median barely moves. Spotting when an outlier makes the mean misleading is an important Grade 6 reasoning skill.
